title: Systems and Higher-Order Equations
short: Rewrite y″ = f(t, y, y′) as a first-order system, then take Euler or Runge–Kutta steps with vectors.
trouble: Students forget that each component needs its own starting value: a second-order equation needs both y(0) and y′(0).

blocks.html: Every one-step method works on vectors as well as numbers. Any higher-order equation becomes a first-order system, as in Systems in Matrix Form, and then Euler, Heun or RK4 run with each $y$ replaced by a vector $\mathbf{u}$ and each $f$ by a vector function $\mathbf{F}$. The error orders stay the same.

To solve $y'' = f(t, y, y')$, set $u_1 = y$, $u_2 = y'$: $$u_1' = u_2,\qquad u_2' = f(t, u_1, u_2).$$ Each component needs its own starting value, so the problem must give both $y(0)$ and $y'(0)$. Then step all components together, always using values from the same stage.

The derivation of each method (Taylor expansion, or averaging slopes) never used that $y$ was a single number; it works component by component. What must not happen is mixing stages: in Euler's method both components of $\mathbf{u}_{n+1}$ are computed from the old $\mathbf{u}_n$. Updating $u_1$ first and then using the new $u_1$ in $u_2$ is a different method, with different behavior.

blocks.title: Euler on an oscillator
blocks.q: For $y'' = -y$, $y(0) = 1$, $y'(0) = 0$, take two Euler steps with $h = 0.1$.
steps: The exact solution keeps $y^{2} + v^{2} = 1$; Euler gives $1$, then $1.01$, then $1.0201$: it multiplies by $1 + h^{2}$ every step, spiraling slowly outward.

blocks.title: Heun does better
blocks.q: Take one Heun step for the same system from $(1, 0)$ with $h = 0.1$.

blocks.name: phaseplane
blocks.cap: The system from the first example: trajectories spiral into the origin as the oscillation dies out. A good numerical method must follow these spirals; Euler with a large step spirals outward instead.

blocks.html: In code, $\mathbf{u}$ is simply an array, and $\mathbf{F}$ returns an array of the same length; the stepping loop does not change at all. Systems also show why stability matters: the components can decay or oscillate at very different rates, set by the eigenvalues of $A$, and a step size must suit all of them. That is the subject of Stability of Euler's Method.

Forgetting that each component needs its own starting value. A second-order equation needs both $y(0)$ and $y'(0)$; an $n$th-order equation needs $n$ values. Without $y'(0)$ the first step of $u_1' = u_2$ cannot even begin. Also keep the stages straight: Euler uses the old values for every component.

sources.name: Tobin A. Driscoll and Richard J. Braun, Fundamentals of Numerical Computation (University of Delaware, free online edition): chapter "Initial-value problems for ODEs", section "IVP systems"
